stages.title: Advanced genetics
stages.hook: In fruit flies, two genes on the same chromosome do not follow Mendel's 9:3:3:1 ratio. How can crosses reveal the distance between genes?
explain: Mendel's law of independent assortment holds for genes on different chromosomes. In a dihybrid cross AaBb × AaBb of unlinked genes with complete dominance, the phenotype ratio is 9:3:3:1. Genes close together on a chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together. Crossing over in meiosis recombines them; the recombination frequency rises with distance, so it is used to build genetic maps: 1% recombination = 1 map unit (centimorgan).

Other patterns extend Mendel. Incomplete dominance gives an intermediate phenotype, codominance shows both alleles (human ABO blood group AB), and multiple alleles exist in a population. Sex-linked genes on the X chromosome give different ratios in males (one X) and females. Epistasis occurs when one gene masks the effect of another. Polygenic traits and the environment give continuous variation.

Pedigrees trace traits through families. Rare recessive autosomal traits often skip generations and affect males and females equally; X-linked recessive traits are seen more often in males, passed from carrier mothers. Population genetics uses the Hardy–Weinberg equations p² + 2pq + q² = 1.

example.q: A test cross of a heterozygous fly (AaBb) with a double recessive (aabb) gives 420 parental and 80 recombinant offspring (total 500). What is the distance between the genes?

analogies.music: Two songs on one album (linked genes) are usually played together, unless the playlist is shuffled by crossing over.
analogies.farm: Breeders map genes near each other to track a trait by a nearby marker.
analogies.tech: Two files saved in the same folder usually move together unless copied separately.

stages.mnemonic: Linked = Lined up together; the farther apart, the more often they split (recombine).
terms: Tendency of genes close on a chromosome to be inherited together.
Fraction of offspring with new allele combinations.
Both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote.
One gene masks or modifies the expression of another.

misc.wrong: A 9:3:3:1 ratio is expected for any two genes.
misc.right: It is expected only when the genes assort independently, such as on different chromosomes or far apart on one chromosome.

stages.limits: Map distance is only approximately proportional to physical distance, and double crossovers make long distances underestimate. Recombination rates also vary along chromosomes.

questions.model: Genes far apart on one chromosome have so many crossovers between them that parental and recombinant gametes become equally frequent, so they behave as unlinked, giving at most 50% recombinants.
questions.why: Frequent crossing over (including double crossovers) saturates at 50%.

panel.q: In a small isolated population, a scientist finds allele frequencies changing from one generation to the next. Which of these is NOT a process that changes allele frequencies?
o: Random mating
Genetic drift
Selection

panel.why: Random mating by itself does not change allele frequencies; it is an assumption of the Hardy–Weinberg model. Drift, selection and migration all alter them.

teach.model: Genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together. Crossing over in meiosis occasionally separates them, producing recombinant offspring. The farther apart two genes are, the more often a crossover falls between them. So the percentage of recombinants measures distance in map units.

stages.title: Genomics
stages.hook: The human genome has about 3.1 billion base pairs, but only about 1–2% codes for proteins. What is the rest doing?
explain: Genomics studies whole genomes. The Human Genome Project produced a reference sequence in 2003, and a complete telomere-to-telomere assembly was published in 2022. Humans have about 20 000 protein-coding genes. Much of the rest includes regulatory regions (promoters, enhancers), non-coding RNA genes, introns and repetitive sequences such as transposable elements.

Sequencing technologies break DNA into reads, which are assembled or aligned to a reference. Coverage (depth) = (number of reads × read length) ÷ genome length. Variants include single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), insertions, deletions and copy-number changes. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) link variants to traits statistically, though association does not imply causation. Comparative genomics reveals conserved sequences that are likely functional.

Individual humans differ at roughly 0.1% of sites. Epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation and histone modifications alter gene activity without changing the DNA sequence. Genomic data raise privacy and fairness questions, because they identify relatives and can reflect biased sampling of populations.

example.q: A 3 Gb genome is sequenced with 600 million reads of 150 bases each. What is the average coverage?

analogies.tech: A genome is a huge shredded book; sequencing reads are scraps and assembly is piecing them back together using overlap.
analogies.city: Most of a city is roads and utilities rather than homes, as most of a genome is not protein-coding.
analogies.music: Gene regulation is like the conductor's marks that decide when each instrument plays.

stages.mnemonic: Genome = the book, genes = the sentences, regulation = the punctuation and stage directions.

A single base-pair difference between individuals.
Average number of times each base is sequenced.

misc.right: Much non-coding DNA is regulatory or encodes functional RNAs, though the fraction that is functional is debated.

stages.limits: Estimates of the functional fraction of the human genome range widely, from a few percent to over 80%, depending on how 'function' is defined.

teach.topic: How a genome is sequenced and what coverage means
teach.model: DNA is cut into small fragments and each is read, giving millions of short reads. They are aligned to a reference or assembled by their overlaps. Coverage is how many times each base is read on average. Higher coverage means errors can be outvoted, so the sequence is more reliable.

stages.title: Biochemistry
stages.hook: ATP releases energy when its terminal phosphate is removed, yet the same bond is not especially strong. Why is the reaction so useful?
explain: Biochemical reactions follow thermodynamics. The Gibbs free energy change ΔG = ΔH − TΔS (T in kelvin) predicts direction: a reaction proceeds spontaneously if ΔG < 0. Cells couple unfavourable (ΔG > 0) reactions to ATP hydrolysis (ΔG about −30 kJ/mol under standard conditions, more negative in cells) so the combined process is favourable.

Enzymes lower activation energy but do not change ΔG or the equilibrium position. Kinetics: v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S]); Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax and indicates affinity (lower Km, higher affinity). Lineweaver–Burk plots 1/v against 1/[S]. Competitive inhibitors raise apparent Km without changing Vmax; non-competitive inhibitors lower Vmax. Allosteric enzymes show sigmoidal kinetics and are regulated by effectors.

Central metabolism: glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate in the cytoplasm with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH; the link reaction and Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix produce CO₂, NADH and FADH₂; the electron transport chain uses these to pump protons across the inner membrane, and ATP synthase uses the proton gradient to make ATP (chemiosmosis). The maximum yield is about 30–32 ATP per glucose.

example.q: A reaction has ΔH = −40 kJ/mol and ΔS = −0.05 kJ/(mol·K). Find ΔG at 300 K.

analogies.tech: ATP is a rechargeable battery that is charged by respiration and discharged to drive work.
analogies.city: Coupling reactions is like using a downhill river to turn a wheel that lifts water uphill.
analogies.farm: A dam holds water that drives turbines, as the proton gradient drives ATP synthase.

stages.mnemonic: Negative ΔG goes: reactions flow downhill; enzymes lower the hill, not the drop.
terms: Energy available to do work; ΔG < 0 means spontaneous.
Substrate concentration giving half the maximum rate.

A favourable reaction driving an unfavourable one.

misc.right: Enzymes change speed only; they do not alter ΔG or the equilibrium position.

stages.limits: ATP yields per glucose are estimates that depend on shuttle systems and proton-to-ATP ratios, which is why sources say 30–32 rather than a single number.

The high-Km enzyme

teach.topic: How the proton gradient makes ATP
teach.model: Electrons from NADH and FADH₂ pass along the electron transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane. The energy released pumps protons across the membrane, making a gradient. Protons flow back through ATP synthase, and this flow drives the formation of ATP from ADP and phosphate.

stages.title: Cellular signalling
stages.hook: A single adrenaline molecule can make a liver cell release thousands of glucose molecules. How can a tiny signal have such a large effect?
explain: Cells communicate with signalling molecules (ligands) that bind to receptors. Steps: reception, transduction and response. Water-soluble ligands (most peptide hormones, adrenaline) bind to cell-surface receptors. Lipid-soluble ligands (steroid hormones) cross the membrane and bind intracellular receptors that act as transcription factors.

G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) activate G proteins, which activate enzymes such as adenylyl cyclase to produce cyclic AMP (cAMP), a second messenger. cAMP activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates target proteins. Each step multiplies the signal, so the cascade amplifies it. Receptor tyrosine kinases dimerise and phosphorylate each other, activating pathways such as Ras–MAPK, which promote cell growth and division.

Signals are switched off by hydrolysis of GTP, breakdown of second messengers (phosphodiesterase breaks down cAMP) and phosphatases that remove phosphate groups. Errors cause disease: mutations that lock Ras on are found in many cancers, and cholera toxin keeps a G protein active, causing severe water loss.

example.q: One activated receptor activates 10 G proteins; each G protein activates 1 adenylyl cyclase, and each cyclase makes 100 cAMP. How many cAMP molecules come from a single receptor?

analogies.tech: A doorbell press triggers a loud bell: small input, big output.
analogies.sport: A coach whistle sets a whole team in motion, with each player relaying the signal.
analogies.city: A single alarm signal from a lookout leads a whole town to respond.

teach.topic: How a small signal is amplified inside a cell
teach.model: A hormone binds a receptor on the cell surface. The receptor activates several G proteins, each activates an enzyme that makes many cAMP molecules. cAMP activates kinases that act on many targets. Each step multiplies the signal, so one hormone molecule can cause a large response.

stages.title: Neuroscience
stages.hook: Neurons are at rest with the inside of the cell about 70 mV more negative than the outside. How does this voltage turn into a signal that travels a metre in milliseconds?
explain: A neuron at rest has a negative resting potential, about −70 mV, maintained by the sodium–potassium pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in) and by leak channels that make the membrane more permeable to K⁺. The equilibrium potential for an ion is given by the Nernst equation: E = (61.5 mV ÷ z) × log₁₀([out] ÷ [in]) at 37 °C.

An action potential is an all-or-nothing event. If depolarisation reaches threshold (about −55 mV), voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes in, then Na⁺ channels inactivate and K⁺ channels open, repolarising the membrane. A refractory period prevents backward propagation. In myelinated axons the impulse jumps between nodes of Ranvier (saltatory conduction), which is faster.

At synapses, an action potential triggers Ca²⁺ entry and release of neurotransmitter, which binds receptors on the next cell. Excitatory inputs (glutamate) depolarise, inhibitory inputs (GABA) hyperpolarise. Neurons add up inputs (summation). Learning involves changes in synaptic strength, such as long-term potentiation. The brain is organised into regions: cortex for higher functions, cerebellum for coordination, brainstem for vital functions.

example.q: Use E = 61.5 × log₁₀([K⁺]out ÷ [K⁺]in) mV with [K⁺]out = 5 mM and [K⁺]in = 140 mM. Find E(K⁺).

analogies.city: A synapse is a relay station where an electrical signal is converted to a chemical message.

teach.model: At rest the inside of the neuron is negative. A stimulus depolarises it to threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and Na⁺ rushes in. stages.title: Developmental biology
stages.hook: A single fertilised egg becomes an animal with hundreds of cell types, all with the same DNA. How do cells know what to become?
explain: Development turns one cell into a patterned organism through cell division, differentiation, morphogenesis and growth. Cells differ not because their DNA differs but because they express different genes. Signalling molecules called morphogens form concentration gradients that tell cells their position; cells respond to different thresholds by activating different genes. In Drosophila, the Bicoid gradient sets up the head–tail axis.

Hox genes encode transcription factors that specify identity along the body axis and are conserved from flies to mammals. Induction occurs when one group of cells signals another to change fate. Stem cells can self-renew and differentiate: embryonic stem cells are pluripotent, adult stem cells are multipotent. Differentiation involves epigenetic changes that stabilise gene expression.

Cells also die in a controlled way, apoptosis, which sculpts structures such as separating fingers and toes. Model organisms (the fruit fly, zebrafish, mouse, nematode worm and the plant Arabidopsis) have taught us general principles. Errors in signalling can cause birth defects; for example, some drugs and toxins disrupt development at specific stages.

example.q: A morphogen concentration falls by half every 100 µm from its source. A gene turns on above 25% of the source concentration. At what distance from the source does the gene switch off?
steps: The threshold is 25%, so the gene is on up to about 200 µm.

analogies.city: Postcodes tell a letter where to go, as morphogen levels tell cells where they are.
analogies.music: The same score played with different instruments gives different parts: same DNA, different expression.
analogies.farm: Soil moisture varies across a field, and crops respond differently along the gradient.

Apoptotic

questions.q: A morphogen halves in concentration every 50 µm. Starting at 100 units at the source, what is the concentration at 150 µm?
A zygote divides with every cell dividing at each round. How many cells after 6 rounds?
A developing hand has 20 000 cells in the webbing between digits, and apoptosis removes 85%. How many cells remain?
A nucleus from an adult cell is placed into an egg with its nucleus removed and a whole animal develops. What does this show?
o: Differentiated cells retain the full genome
Specialised cells lose genes as they develop
Eggs contain no DNA of their own
Cloning of animals is impossible
questions.why: Nuclear transfer demonstrates genomic equivalence.

questions.q: A mutant fly has legs growing where antennae should be. Which gene type is probably affected?
o: A Hox (homeotic) gene
A metabolic enzyme gene
A ribosomal gene
A gene for eye pigment
questions.why: Homeotic mutations transform body parts.

questions.q: Order the developmental events.
questions.why: Early cell divisions precede formation of germ layers and organs.

questions.q: Match each process to its role.
pairs: Stem cell makes more stem cells
questions.why: Different mechanisms build the embryo.

questions.q: Explain how a morphogen gradient can lead to several different cell types across a tissue.
questions.model: Cells at different distances from the source receive different morphogen concentrations. Different concentration thresholds switch on different genes, so cells at different positions adopt different fates.
questions.why: Thresholds convert a continuous gradient into discrete cell types.

panel.q: Why might a drug cause the most harm to the embryo at a specific stage?
o: Particular structures form during critical windows
Embryos have no cells to be harmed at that stage
Drugs only work at night during pregnancy
All embryonic stages are identical in their risk
panel.why: Critical periods of organ formation make timing important.

panel.q: Adult stem cells in bone marrow make blood cells but not neurons in normal conditions. They are:
o: Multipotent
Pluripotent
Totipotent
Differentiated into nerve
panel.why: Their potential is limited to a range of related cell types.

panel.q: Why are similar developmental genes found in flies and mice?
o: They inherited them from a common ancestor
It happened by chance alone
Flies copied the genes from mice
The genes are identical in all animals and plants
panel.why: Deep conservation reflects shared ancestry.

teach.topic: How cells with the same DNA become different
teach.model: All cells carry the same genome, but different genes are switched on. Signals such as morphogens form gradients, so cells at different positions get different amounts. These levels switch on different transcription factors and genes, giving each cell its fate.

points.ask: How do cells know where they are?

stages.title: Biotechnology
stages.hook: Bacteria can be engineered to make human insulin. How do you move a gene from one species to another and get it to work?
explain: Recombinant DNA technology cuts DNA with restriction enzymes at specific sequences, often leaving sticky ends, and joins pieces with DNA ligase. A gene is inserted into a vector such as a plasmid, introduced into host cells (transformation), and cells carrying it are selected, for example with an antibiotic resistance marker. The host then expresses the gene, as bacteria do for human insulin.

PCR amplifies DNA through repeated cycles of denaturation (about 95 °C), annealing of primers (about 55–65 °C) and extension by a heat-stable polymerase (about 72 °C). Ideal amplification doubles the DNA each cycle, giving 2ⁿ copies after n cycles. Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size: smaller fragments move farther through the gel toward the positive electrode.

CRISPR–Cas9 uses a guide RNA to direct the Cas9 nuclease to a matching DNA sequence, making a cut that cells repair; researchers can disrupt a gene or, with a template, edit it. Applications include medicines, crops with improved traits, and diagnostics. Ethical questions concern safety, consent, fairness of access, environmental release and heritable human editing, which most countries restrict.

example.q: Starting from 1 DNA molecule, ideal PCR for 10 cycles gives how many copies?

analogies.tech: Restriction enzymes are like scissors, ligase is glue, a plasmid is a USB stick carrying new instructions.
analogies.farm: Selective breeding takes generations; genetic engineering moves specific genes directly.
analogies.home: PCR is like a photocopier that doubles the pages each cycle.

stages.mnemonic: Cut, Paste, Copy, Check: restriction enzyme, ligase, PCR, gel.
terms: Enzyme that cuts DNA at a specific sequence.
Circular DNA used as a vector.
Technique that makes many copies of a DNA segment.
A system that cuts DNA at a site chosen by a guide RNA.

misc.wrong: Genetically engineered foods always contain DNA that other foods lack.
misc.right: All foods contain DNA. The question is which genes and traits have been changed, and each product is assessed for safety individually.

stages.limits: Off-target edits, unequal access to therapies and ecological effects of released organisms are active areas of debate and regulation.

trip.prompt: Find how Cas9 is guided to its target sequence and what the cell does after the cut.

questions.q: Which enzyme joins DNA fragments together?
o: DNA ligase
Restriction enzyme
Helicase
Taq polymerase
questions.why: Ligase seals the sugar–phosphate backbone.

questions.q: Ideal PCR starts with 5 DNA molecules. How many copies after 8 cycles?
A plasmid of 5000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at two sites giving one fragment of 1200 bp and another. What is the size of the other fragment?
In gel electrophoresis, which DNA fragments travel farthest?
o: The smallest
The largest
All the same
Those with the most G–C
questions.why: Small fragments move through the gel more easily.

questions.q: Why is a heat-stable polymerase used in PCR?
o: It survives the repeated heating to about 95 °C
It copies only RNA in the sample
It is cheaper than other polymerases to buy
It works only when it is kept in the cold
questions.why: Taq polymerase is not denatured at high temperature.

questions.q: Bacteria transformed with a plasmid carrying an ampicillin resistance gene are grown on ampicillin plates. Why?
o: Only bacteria that took up the plasmid survive
To kill the plasmid as it enters the cell
To make insulin faster in the culture
To increase the PCR yield from the sample
questions.why: Antibiotics select for transformed cells.

questions.q: Order the steps of one PCR cycle.
questions.why: Each cycle includes these steps and doubles the target.

questions.q: Match the tool to its function.
pairs: Cuts DNA at a specific site
questions.why: Each tool plays a role in genetic engineering.

questions.q: A company wants to produce human insulin in bacteria. Describe the main steps.
questions.model: Isolate the human insulin gene, cut it and a plasmid with the same restriction enzyme, join them with ligase, insert the plasmid into bacteria, select the transformed cells, then grow them in a fermenter and purify the insulin.
questions.why: Recombinant DNA workflow.

questions.q: Heritable germline editing in humans is restricted in many countries mainly because:
o: Changes pass to future generations who cannot consent, and safety is uncertain
DNA cannot be cut by any enzyme in the lab, so edits fail
It is far too cheap, so everyone would use it
It affects only plants, not animals, so it needs no laws
questions.why: Ethical and safety concerns are major.

panel.q: A forensic lab amplifies DNA from a tiny sample. A risk is contamination. Why is PCR especially vulnerable?
o: It exponentially amplifies any DNA present, including contaminants
It destroys DNA so contaminants are removed first
It works only with RNA samples
It cannot amplify very small samples of DNA at all
panel.why: Small amounts of stray DNA are copied too.

panel.q: A gene-edited crop is released. Which concern requires ecological testing?
o: Gene flow to wild relatives
Photosynthesis stops in the crop
Roots of the crop become metal
DNA of the crop turns into RNA
panel.why: Transfer of traits to wild plants could alter ecosystems.

panel.q: Why can eukaryotic genes with introns not be directly expressed in bacteria from genomic DNA?
o: Bacteria cannot splice introns
Bacteria lack DNA to start with
Introns are proteins that bacteria destroy
Genes are always too short in bacteria
panel.why: cDNA made from mRNA is used instead.

teach.model: PCR heats DNA to separate the strands, cools it so short primers can attach to the target, then a heat-stable polymerase builds new strands from each primer. Every cycle doubles the number of copies, so after 30 cycles there are about a billion copies of the starting piece.

points.ask: How many copies do you get?

stages.title: Bioinformatics
stages.hook: You find a new gene in a bacterium. How can a computer tell you what it probably does, using only its sequence?
explain: Bioinformatics uses computation to analyse biological data. Sequences are stored in public databases such as GenBank and UniProt. Pairwise alignment compares sequences to find similarity; BLAST searches databases for matches and reports an E-value, the number of matches with at least that score expected by chance. Smaller E-values indicate more significant matches. High sequence similarity suggests homology (common ancestry), which often implies similar function, but this is an inference.

Multiple sequence alignments reveal conserved residues and are used to build phylogenetic trees. Gene finders predict genes by signals such as start codons, open reading frames (ORFs) and splice sites. GC content is the fraction of bases that are G or C. Transcriptomics (RNA-seq) counts reads to estimate gene expression; normalisation is needed, for example reads per million, before comparing samples.

Data analysis requires careful statistics. Testing thousands of genes at once means many false positives by chance, so p-values must be corrected for multiple testing (for example Bonferroni: divide the threshold by the number of tests). Machine learning methods such as protein structure prediction have advanced rapidly but depend on training data and need experimental validation.

example.q: In an RNA-seq sample, gene X has 500 reads out of 20 million total reads. Compute reads per million (RPM).

analogies.tech: BLAST is a search engine for sequences.
analogies.city: Alignment is like lining up two maps to find matching roads.
analogies.sport: Normalisation is like comparing goals per match rather than raw goals.

stages.mnemonic: Search, Align, Count, Correct: BLAST, MSA, RNA-seq, multiple testing.
terms: Arranging sequences to show regions of similarity.
Expected number of equally good matches by chance.
A stretch of sequence that could be translated, from a start to a stop codon.
Adjusting thresholds when many tests are done.

misc.wrong: A sequence match always proves the same function.
misc.right: A strong match suggests a shared ancestor and probably similar function, but function must be confirmed experimentally.

stages.limits: Databases contain annotation errors that propagate when predictions are copied from entry to entry.

trip.prompt: Find how an E-value is interpreted and why smaller values are better.

questions.q: A BLAST hit has E = 10⁻⁵⁰. What does this mean?
o: Such a match is extremely unlikely by chance
The match is certainly wrong
The two sequences are identical
The query sequence must be RNA
questions.why: A tiny E-value means high significance.

questions.q: A DNA sequence is 200 bases long and 120 of them are G or C. What is its GC content?
Gene Y has 300 reads in a library of 15 million. Compute reads per million.
A study tests 2000 genes at α = 0.05. Using Bonferroni, what per-gene threshold should be used?
If 2000 independent tests each have a 5% chance of a false positive and no real effects exist, about how many false positives are expected?
o: About 100
About 5
About 2000
None

questions.q: A gene shares 80% identity with a well-studied enzyme in another species. A cautious conclusion is that it:
o: Probably has a similar function but needs testing
Certainly has the same function in both species
Is totally unrelated to the other enzyme
Is a pseudogene that does nothing at all
questions.why: Homology suggests function; confirmation needed.

questions.q: An ORF finder reads a DNA sequence in all six frames. Why six?
o: Three frames on each of the two strands
Six chromosomes are present in each cell
Six different amino acids are coded
Six start codons exist in the genetic code
questions.why: Each strand can be read in three frames.

questions.q: Order a simple RNA-seq analysis.
questions.why: Reads are counted and normalised before comparing.

questions.q: Match each tool to its purpose.
pairs: Search a database for similar sequences
questions.why: Different tools answer different questions.

questions.q: Why must results be corrected when thousands of genes are tested at once?
questions.model: With thousands of tests, many genes would appear significant by chance alone, so the significance threshold is adjusted (for example Bonferroni or false discovery rate) to control false positives.
questions.why: Multiple testing inflates false positives.

panel.q: A database annotation says protein Z is a kinase, but it was inferred only from sequence similarity to another computer-annotated entry. What is the problem?
o: Errors can propagate through database chains
Kinases are not proteins
Databases never contain proteins at all
Sequence similarity is impossible to measure
panel.why: Unverified annotations spread errors.

panel.q: Two RNA-seq samples have 10 million and 40 million reads. A gene has 100 reads in each. Which is correct?
o: Its expression is higher in the smaller library
It is exactly the same in both samples
It is higher in the larger library
It cannot be compared between the samples
panel.why: 100 reads in 10 M is 10 RPM; in 40 M it is 2.5 RPM.

panel.q: A machine learning model predicts protein structures from sequence. Which caution applies?
o: Predictions need experimental validation and depend on training data
They are always perfect and need no checking
They replace the need for all experiments
They work only on DNA sequences, not on proteins
panel.why: Models can be wrong, especially for unusual proteins.

teach.model: BLAST compares a query sequence with a database and finds the closest matching sequences. It reports an E-value, the number of matches that good you would expect by chance. A very small E-value means the match is likely real, which suggests the genes share an ancestor and may have a similar function.

points.ask: How do you know a match is real?

stages.title: Conservation biology and environmental change
stages.hook: Species are being lost faster than the typical background rate. How do scientists measure biodiversity, and which actions work best?
explain: Biodiversity has genetic, species and ecosystem levels. Species diversity is measured by richness (number of species) and by indices that also consider evenness, such as Simpson's index D = 1 − Σ(n/N)², where n is the number of individuals of each species and N the total. D near 1 means high diversity.

Main threats are habitat loss and fragmentation, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution and climate change. Small populations are at risk from genetic drift, inbreeding and chance events (extinction vortex). Conservation strategies include protected areas, wildlife corridors, captive breeding and reintroduction, restoring habitat, sustainable management and working with Indigenous and local communities, whose lands often hold high biodiversity. The IUCN Red List classifies species by extinction risk.

Climate change shifts the ranges and timing of species. Atmospheric CO₂ has risen from about 280 ppm before industrialisation to over 420 ppm, mainly from fossil fuels and land-use change. Oceans absorb CO₂ and become more acidic. Ecosystem services (pollination, clean water, carbon storage) show how biodiversity supports people. Solutions need evidence, local participation and fairness.

example.q: A sample has 50 individuals of species A, 30 of B and 20 of C. Calculate Simpson's diversity index D = 1 − Σ(n/N)².

analogies.farm: Planting many crop varieties spreads risk against disease, as genetic diversity buffers a species.
analogies.city: A city with many kinds of businesses is more resilient than one dependent on a single factory.
analogies.tech: Backups in several locations protect data, as many species protect an ecosystem's functions.

stages.mnemonic: HIPPO threats: Habitat loss, Invasives, Pollution, Population (human), Overharvest, plus climate.
terms: The number of different species in an area.
Breaking of habitat into small isolated patches.
Feedback in which small populations become more vulnerable.

misc.wrong: Conservation means keeping nature free of people.
misc.right: Many successful programmes involve local and Indigenous communities and sustainable use, not only exclusion.

stages.limits: Extinction rate estimates vary with methods, and many species, especially invertebrates, are undescribed, so the true scale is uncertain.

trip.prompt: Find the Red List categories and place one species you know into one.

questions.q: A sample has 40 individuals of species A and 60 of species B. Calculate Simpson's D = 1 − Σ(n/N)².
A sample has 4 equally abundant species with 25 individuals each. Calculate D = 1 − Σ(n/N)².
CO₂ rose from 280 ppm to 420 ppm. What is the percentage increase?
Which sample is more diverse by Simpson's index: species counts 50, 50 or counts 95, 5?
o: 50, 50 (higher evenness)
95, 5, because one species dominates
Both samples are identical in diversity
The samples cannot be compared at all

questions.q: Why do wildlife corridors help conserve fragmented populations?
o: They allow movement and gene flow between patches
They remove the predators from every patch
They increase pollution in the patches
They isolate the patches from one another
questions.why: Connectivity reduces inbreeding and local extinction.

questions.q: An invasive predator is introduced to an island with prey that evolved without predators. What is the likely result?
o: Rapid decline of naive prey species
No change, since the prey cope easily
More prey, since they are not used to predators
Prey evolve instantly to resist the predator
questions.why: Prey lacking defences are vulnerable.

questions.q: Order the IUCN Red List categories from lowest to highest extinction risk.
questions.why: Risk rises across these categories.

questions.q: Match the threat to a conservation response.
questions.why: Responses should match the cause.

questions.q: Explain why very small populations are at high risk of extinction even if the original cause of decline stops.
questions.model: Small populations lose genetic diversity through drift and inbreeding, and random events such as disease or poor breeding years can wipe them out. These effects reinforce one another in an extinction vortex.
questions.why: Small size creates self-reinforcing risks.

questions.q: Ocean acidification is mainly caused by:
o: Absorption of atmospheric CO₂ by seawater
Oil spills at sea on the surface
Warming of the water alone
Salt running off from the land
questions.why: CO₂ dissolves to form carbonic acid, lowering pH.

panel.q: A reserve protects a forest but local people lose access to resources without compensation. What does evidence suggest about long-term success?
o: It is often less successful without local support and fairness
It is always successful, whatever the local people think
People never matter to a conservation project
Forests do not need protection from anyone
panel.why: Community involvement improves conservation outcomes.

panel.q: A species is lost from an ecosystem but the total species richness stays the same because a new invader arrived. Why is richness alone misleading?
o: It ignores species identity and function
Richness is always an accurate measure of ecosystem health
Invaders always add the services that were lost
Richness counts individuals rather than species
panel.why: Different species have different roles and values.

panel.q: Mangrove forests are protected as coastal defences and fish nurseries. This is an argument based on:
o: Ecosystem services
Genetic drift in small populations
Speciation of new fish
Mutation of the mangrove genes
panel.why: They provide benefits to people.

teach.model: Species richness counts the species. Simpson's index also considers how evenly individuals are spread: add the squares of each species' proportion and subtract from 1. A community with many species of similar abundance has a value close to 1.

points.ask: How do you read the index?
